questions.question: Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error. The patient had been waiting patiently for over two hours before the doctor finally attends to him for a check-up.
questions.questionHtml:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

The patient had been waiting patiently for over two hours before the doctor finally attends to him for a check-up.
questions.solution:
The error is in the verb tense in the segment "finally attends". The first part of the sentence uses the Past Perfect Continuous tense (had been waiting), which describes an action that was ongoing for a duration before another event in the past. This sets the entire context of the sentence in the past. The second action must also be in the past tense.

The verb 'attends' is in the Simple Present tense, which is incorrect. It should be in the Simple Past tense ('attended') to maintain the correct sequence of tenses.

Correct sentence: The patient had been waiting patiently for over two hours before the doctor finally attended to him for a check-up.

Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. By this time next year, my sister ________ her master's degree from the university.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

By this time next year, my sister ________ her master's degree from the university.
questions.solution:
The given sentence describes an action that will be finished before a specific point in the future. The key phrase is "By this time next year," which sets a future deadline for the completion of an action. Therefore, the blank requires a verb in the Future Perfect tense.

The correct option is "will have completed". The Future Perfect tense (will + have + past participle) is used to express an action that will be finished by a certain future time. It perfectly fits the context of completing a degree by a future date.

The other options do not fit:

· "will complete" (Simple Future) indicates that the action will happen in the future but doesn't emphasize its completion before a specific time.

· "is completing" (Present Continuous) is used for an action happening now, which contradicts the future timeline.

· "completed" (Simple Past) refers to an action that is already finished, which is incorrect.

Thus, the correct sentence is: "By this time next year, my sister will have completed her master's degree from the university."

Hence, option (c) is the answer.

questions.question: Select the option with the correct use of future tense.
questions.questionHtml: Select the option with the correct use of future tense.

options.text: If the weather forecast is accurate, it is going to snow heavily tomorrow.
options.html: If the weather forecast is accurate, it is going to snow heavily tomorrow.

options.text: If the weather forecast is accurate, it will have snowed heavily tomorrow.
options.html: If the weather forecast is accurate, it will have snowed heavily tomorrow.

options.text: If the weather forecast will be accurate, it is going to snow heavily tomorrow.
options.html: If the weather forecast will be accurate, it is going to snow heavily tomorrow.

options.text: If the weather forecast is accurate, it will have been snowing heavily tomorrow.
options.html: If the weather forecast is accurate, it will have been snowing heavily tomorrow.

questions.solution:
The correct option is a) If the weather forecast is accurate, it is going to snow heavily tomorrow.

This sentence is a Type 1 conditional sentence, used for real future possibilities. The structure is If + Simple Present, ... Simple Future. The phrase "is going to" is a common way to express the simple future, especially for predictions based on present evidence (the accurate forecast).

Let's look at why the other options are incorrect:

· Option (b): This uses the future perfect tense ("will have snowed"), which is incorrect. It would mean the snowing will be finished by some point tomorrow, which is not the intended meaning of a general prediction.

· Option (c): This is incorrect because the 'if' clause in a Type 1 conditional must use the simple present tense ("is"), not the future tense ("will be").

· Option (d): This uses the future perfect continuous tense, which is incorrect as it describes the duration of an action up to a future point, not a simple prediction.

questions.question: Select a grammatically correct sentence using the future tense.
questions.questionHtml: Select a grammatically correct sentence using the future tense.

options.text: As soon as the sun will set, the streetlights will turn on automatically.
options.html: As soon as the sun will set, the streetlights will turn on automatically.

options.text: As soon as the sun sets, the streetlights will turn on automatically.
options.html: As soon as the sun sets, the streetlights will turn on automatically.

options.text: As soon as the sun will set, the streetlights are turning on automatically.
options.html: As soon as the sun will set, the streetlights are turning on automatically.

options.text: As soon as the sun has set, the streetlights would turn on automatically.
options.html: As soon as the sun has set, the streetlights would turn on automatically.

questions.solution:
The correct option is b) As soon as the sun sets, the streetlights will turn on automatically.

This sentence demonstrates the correct structure for future time clauses. When a clause begins with a time conjunction like "as soon as," "when," "before," or "after" and refers to the future, it must use the simple present tense ("sets"). The main clause then uses the simple future tense ("will turn on").

Let's look at why the other options are incorrect:

· Option (a): This is incorrect because the future tense ("will set") cannot be used in a future time clause starting with "as soon as".

· Option (c): This has two errors: it incorrectly uses the future tense in the time clause and uses the present continuous tense ("are turning on") in the main clause, which is less appropriate than the simple future for a statement of future fact.

· Option (d): This has two errors: it incorrectly uses the present perfect ("has set") in the time clause and "would" instead of "will" in the main clause.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. If I knew his address, I (would have visited his) home to meet his parents.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

If I knew his address, I (would have visited his) home to meet his parents.
questions.solution:
This sentence is a Type 2 conditional, used for hypothetical or unreal situations in the present. The 'if' clause uses the Simple Past tense ("knew") to express this unreality. The main clause (the result clause) in a Type 2 conditional must use "would" + the base form of the verb. The underlined segment incorrectly uses "would have visited," which belongs to a Type 3 conditional (for unreal past situations).

The correct option is "would visit his" because it follows the correct structure for a Type 2 conditional ("would" + base verb).

Option b) "will visit his" is used for Type 1 conditionals (real future possibilities).

Option c) "would be visiting his" implies an ongoing action, which is less appropriate here than the simple result.

Option d) "will have visited his" is the Future Perfect tense and doesn't fit the conditional structure.

So, the correct sentence is: If I knew his address, I would visit his home to meet his parents.

Hence, the most appropriate choice is a) would visit his.

questions.question: Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error. It is high time that the municipal corporation realises its responsibility towards maintaining the cleanliness of the city's public parks.
questions.questionHtml:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

It is high time that the municipal corporation realises its responsibility towards maintaining the cleanliness of the city's public parks.
questions.solution:
The error is in the verb tense in the segment "realises". The idiomatic expression "It is time" or "It is high time" is followed by a subject and a verb in the Simple Past tense. This structure is used to express that something should have been done earlier and is overdue.

The verb realises is in the Simple Present tense. The correct verb form to use in this structure is the Simple Past tense, which is 'realised'.

Correct sentence:

It is high time that the municipal corporation realised its responsibility towards maintaining the cleanliness of the city's public parks.

Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. He ________ to the gym every single morning before he goes to work.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

He ________ to the gym every single morning before he goes to work.
questions.solution:
The sentence describes a routine or habitual action. The phrases "every single morning" and "before he goes to work" are key indicators of a repeated, daily habit. The blank requires a verb tense that expresses regular, habitual actions in the present.

The correct option is "goes". The Simple Present tense is used to describe habits, routines, and general truths. Since going to the gym is a daily routine for him, the Simple Present is the most appropriate choice.

The other options do not fit:

· "is going" (Present Continuous) would imply he is on his way to the gym right now, not that it's a habit.

· "went" (Simple Past) refers to a completed action in the past.

· "has gone" (Present Perfect) indicates a recent past action with a result in the present, not a routine.

Thus, the correct sentence is: "He goes to the gym every single morning before he goes to work."

Hence, option (a) is the answer.

questions.question: Select the option with the correct use of the present tense.
questions.questionHtml: Select the option with the correct use of the present tense.

options.text: The Earth is revolving around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
options.html: The Earth is revolving around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.

options.text: The Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
options.html: The Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.

options.text: The Earth has revolved around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.
options.html: The Earth has revolved around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.

options.text: The Earth has been revolving around the Sun since an elliptical orbit.
options.html: The Earth has been revolving around the Sun since an elliptical orbit.

questions.solution:
The correct option is b) The Earth revolves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit.

This sentence correctly uses the simple present tense (revolves). The simple present tense is used to state universal truths, scientific facts, and general habits that are always true. The fact that the Earth orbits the Sun is a universal truth.

Let's look at why the other options are incorrect:

· Option (a): This uses the present continuous tense ("is revolving"). This tense is used for actions happening right now or for temporary situations, not for permanent universal truths.

· Option (c): This uses the present perfect tense ("has revolved"), which implies a recently completed action or an action with a result in the present. This is inappropriate for a timeless fact.

· Option (d): This uses the present perfect continuous tense incorrectly. "Since" must be followed by a point in time, not a description of the orbit like "an elliptical orbit".

questions.question: Select the option with the correct use of the present tense.
questions.questionHtml: Select the option with the correct use of the present tense.

options.text: Look! That talented artist is painting a beautiful landscape on the canvas.
options.html: Look! That talented artist is painting a beautiful landscape on the canvas.

options.text: Look! That talented artist paints a beautiful landscape on the canvas.
options.html: Look! That talented artist paints a beautiful landscape on the canvas.

options.text: Look! That talented artist has painted a beautiful landscape on the canvas.
options.html: Look! That talented artist has painted a beautiful landscape on the canvas.

options.text: Look! That talented artist has been painting a beautiful landscape on the canvas.
options.html: Look! That talented artist has been painting a beautiful landscape on the canvas.

questions.solution:
The correct option is a) Look! That talented artist is painting a beautiful landscape on the canvas.

This sentence correctly uses the present continuous tense (is painting). The word "Look!" at the beginning of the sentence indicates that the action is happening at the moment of speaking. The present continuous tense is the correct choice for describing actions in progress right now.

Let's look at why the other options are incorrect:

· Option (b): This uses the simple present tense ("paints"), which is used for habits or general truths, not for an action happening at this specific moment.

· Option (c): This uses the present perfect tense ("has painted"), which would imply the action is already finished. The word "Look!" suggests the action is ongoing.

· Option (d): This uses the present perfect continuous tense ("has been painting"). While it describes an ongoing action, it emphasizes the duration from a past point until now, which is not the primary focus here. The simple present continuous is more direct.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. The board demanded that the new policy (is implemented immediately) by the manager.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

The board demanded that the new policy (is implemented immediately) by the manager.
questions.solution:
The sentence uses a verb of command or demand ("demanded"). In such cases, the clause that follows (the 'that' clause) must use the subjunctive mood. In the present subjunctive, the base form of the verb (the infinitive without 'to') is used, regardless of the subject. Here, the verb is "to be," so its base form is "be".

The correct option is "be implemented immediately" because it correctly uses the subjunctive mood ("be" + past participle for passive voice).

Option a) "was implemented immediately" is the Simple Past and is incorrect.

Option c) "has been implemented immediately" is the Present Perfect and is incorrect.

Option d) "will be implemented immediately" is the future tense and is not in the subjunctive mood.

So, the correct sentence is: The board demanded that the new policy be implemented immediately by the manager.

Hence, the most appropriate choice is b) be implemented immediately.

questions.question: Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error. If the city's administration had taken stricter measures earlier, the waterlogging situation will not have become so severe after the heavy rainfall .
questions.questionHtml:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

If the city's administration had taken stricter measures earlier, the waterlogging situation will not have become so severe after the heavy rainfall.
questions.solution:
The error is in the main clause of this Type 3 conditional sentence in the segment will not have become. Type 3 conditionals are used to talk about unreal past situations. The structure is: If + Past Perfect, ... would/could/might + have + Past Participle (V3).

The 'if' clause (If the city's administration had taken...) correctly uses the Past Perfect tense. Therefore, the main clause must use "would have + V3", not "will have + V3".

Correct sentence: If the city's administration had taken stricter measures earlier, the waterlogging situation would not have become so severe after the heavy rainfall.

Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

questions.question: Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error. My cousin is working as a software developer in that multinational company since he graduated from college two years ago.
questions.questionHtml:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

My cousin is working as a software developer in that multinational company since he graduated from college two years ago.
questions.solution:
The error is in the use of the Present Continuous tense in the segment is working. The sentence uses the conjunction 'since' to indicate a point in the past ('he graduated') from which an action has continued up to the present. For such actions that start in the past and continue to the present, the Present Perfect Continuous tense ('has been working') or the Present Perfect tense ('has worked') should be used. The Present Continuous tense ('is working') is typically used for actions happening right now or in the current period, but not with 'since' to denote duration from a past point.

Correct sentence: My cousin has been working as a software developer in that multinational company since he graduated from college two years ago.

Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. I cannot come to the phone right now because I ________ a shower.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I cannot come to the phone right now because I ________ a shower.
questions.solution:
The sentence explains the reason for a current inability ("I cannot come to the phone right now"). The reason is an action that is in progress at the moment of speaking. The blank requires a verb tense that describes an action happening at the present moment.

The correct option is "am taking". The Present Continuous tense (am/is/are + -ing) is used to describe actions that are happening at the time of speaking. The speaker is currently in the shower, which is why they cannot answer the phone.

The other options do not fit:

· "took" (Simple Past) describes a completed action in the past.

· "had taken" (Past Perfect) describes an action completed before another past action.

· "have taken" (Present Perfect) describes a recently completed action, but the context implies the action is still ongoing.

Thus, the correct sentence is: "I cannot come to the phone right now because I am taking a shower."

Hence, option (d) is the answer.

questions.question: Select the option with the correct use of the past tense.
questions.questionHtml: Select the option with the correct use of the past tense.

options.text: While I was studying for my exam, my phone rang loudly.
options.html: While I was studying for my exam, my phone rang loudly.

options.text: While I had been studying for my exam, my phone rang loudly.
options.html: While I had been studying for my exam, my phone rang loudly.

options.text: While I studied for my exam, my phone had rung loudly.
options.html: While I studied for my exam, my phone had rung loudly.

options.text: While I was studying for my exam, my phone was ringing loudly.
options.html: While I was studying for my exam, my phone was ringing loudly.

questions.solution:
The correct option is a) While I was studying for my exam, my phone rang loudly.

This sentence correctly uses the past continuous tense (was studying) for a longer, background action and the simple past tense (rang) for a shorter, interrupting action. This is the standard structure for showing an interruption in the past.

Let's look at why the other options are incorrect:

· Option (b): This uses the past perfect continuous ("had been studying"), which is not necessary here as there is no earlier past action to refer to.

· Option (c): This incorrectly uses the simple past ("studied") for the longer action and the past perfect ("had rung") for the interrupting action.

· Option (d): This uses the past continuous for both actions ("was studying" and "was ringing"), which suggests two parallel, ongoing actions rather than one interrupting the other.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence. Our guide explained that the sun (had risen in the east) every single day.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the bracketed segment in the given sentence.

Our guide explained that the sun (had risen in the east) every single day.
questions.solution:
The sentence is in indirect (reported) speech. While the reporting verb "explained" is in the past, the information in the 'that' clause ("the sun... in the east") is a universal truth or a scientific fact. A universal truth is always expressed in the Simple Present tense, even when the reporting verb is in the past. The underlined part incorrectly uses the Past Perfect tense ("had risen").

The correct option is "rises in the east," which uses the Simple Present tense to state the universal fact.

Option a) "is rising in the east" is Present Continuous and implies a temporary action.

Option c) "has risen in the east" is Present Perfect and is not used for universal truths.

Option d) "was rising in the east" is Past Continuous and incorrect.

So, the correct sentence is: Our guide explained that the sun rises in the east every single day.

Hence, the most appropriate choice is b) rises in the east.

questions.question: Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error. The research team has submitted its detailed report about the project's progress to the management committee last week.
questions.questionHtml:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

The research team has submitted its detailed report about the project's progress to the management committee last week.
questions.solution:
The error is in the use of the Present Perfect tense in the segment "has submitted". The sentence contains the specific past time adverbial 'last week', which indicates that the action was completed at a definite time in the past. For actions completed at a specific past time, the Simple Past tense should be used.

The correct verb form is 'submitted' (V2 form of submit). The Present Perfect tense ('has submitted') is used for actions that have a connection to the present or occurred at an unspecified time in the past.

Correct sentence: The research team submitted its detailed report about the project's progress to the management committee last week.

Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. While the children ________ in the park, their parents were watching them from a bench.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

While the children ________ in the park, their parents were watching them from a bench.
questions.solution:
The sentence describes two simultaneous actions that were happening at the same time in the past. The conjunction "While" signals that two ongoing actions are occurring concurrently. The second clause ("their parents were watching") is in the Past Continuous tense, indicating an ongoing past action. The blank requires a verb tense that matches this for a parallel, ongoing action.

The correct option is "were playing". The Past Continuous tense (was/were + -ing) is used to describe an ongoing action at a specific time in the past, or two ongoing actions happening at the same time. It perfectly parallels the action of "were watching."

The other options do not fit:

· "had played" (Past Perfect) would mean they finished playing before the parents watched them.

· "have played" (Present Perfect) is a present tense and cannot be used in this past context.

· "played" (Simple Past) would describe a completed action, not one happening simultaneously with another ongoing action.

Thus, the correct sentence is: "While the children were playing in the park, their parents were watching them from a bench."

Hence, option (a) is the answer.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. It is imperative that every applicant ________ a copy of their portfolio with the submission.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

It is imperative that every applicant ________ a copy of their portfolio with the submission.
questions.solution:
The given sentence expresses a strong command or necessity. The phrase "It is imperative that..." triggers the use of the subjunctive mood, which is used for demands, suggestions, wishes, or hypothetical situations. In the present subjunctive, the base form of the verb (the infinitive without 'to') is used for all subjects.

The correct option is "include". Even though the subject "every applicant" is grammatically singular, the subjunctive mood requires the base form of the verb. Therefore, "include" is correct instead of the simple present "includes".

The other options do not fit:

· "includes" (Simple Present) would be the standard choice in a regular declarative sentence, but it is incorrect here due to the subjunctive trigger.

· "is including" (Present Continuous) is incorrect as it describes an ongoing action, not a requirement.

· "included" (Simple Past) is incorrect as the sentence refers to a present or future requirement.

Thus, the correct sentence is: "It is imperative that every applicant include a copy of their portfolio with the submission."

Hence, option (c) is the answer.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. He looked utterly exhausted when I saw him as he (drove for ten straight) hours.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

He looked utterly exhausted when I saw him as he (drove for ten straight) hours.

options.text: had been driving for ten straight
options.html: had been driving for ten straight

questions.solution:
The sentence explains the reason for a state in the past ("He looked utterly exhausted"). The reason is an action that was ongoing for a long duration ("for ten straight hours") and had just finished or was finishing before the moment of observation ("when I saw him"). This context requires a tense that emphasizes the continuous nature and duration of a past action that occurred before another past event.

The correct option is "had been driving for ten straight". The Past Perfect Continuous tense (had + been + -ing) is the most precise choice here because it perfectly emphasizes the prolonged, continuous activity (driving) that led to the visible result (exhaustion) in the past.

Option a) "was driving for ten straight" (Past Continuous) would imply he was still driving at the exact moment I saw him, which doesn't fit the context as well.

Option b) "has been driving for ten" (Present Perfect Continuous) is incorrect because the entire narrative is set in the past.

Option d) "has driven for ten straight" (Present Perfect) is incorrect because the entire narrative is set in the past.

So, the correct sentence is: He looked utterly exhausted when I saw him, as he had been driving for ten straight hours.

Hence, the most appropriate choice is c) had been driving for ten straight.
